section.title: John White: Promotion Culture, Meta Teams, and Career Regrets
section.deck: John White describes how promotion incentives shaped Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization teams, why he treats team culture as a choice, and what he regrets most.

blocks.text: In John White's view, big-tech promotion systems reward a visible career story more than the work itself. He says that in Meta's AI infrastructure and monetization groups, promotion goals pushed teams to ship projects many people expected to fail, and to build systems tightly coupled to other systems, because a rollout that touched many systems helped with promotion. He argues that engineers still have real agency to choose a healthier team, even though that choice can mean slower promotion and lower pay. Editorially, the rest of the conversation covers his early years on experimentation tools, the cost of treating industry as a fallback, statistics and A/B testing rigor, and his regrets.
blocks.heading: John White's view: promotion incentives, not only pay, steer what engineers build and how teams work

blocks.question: Is John still bullish on Meta and MSL after working there from the inside?
answer: John says he is very bullish on Meta as a company, now as a stockholder rather than an employee. He is much less bullish about being an employee who holds little equity, which he says describes most people, since most staff are paid mostly in cash.

He says working at Meta is less enjoyable than before, even though the business is run very well for the bottom line. He keeps investing in the company and expects to continue. He describes being an employee there as a more stressful time than before.

followups.question: What makes being an employee harder now?
answer: John says the labor market for engineers has shifted across Silicon Valley. Employers once made large sacrifices to keep scarce engineers. Outside a small set of AI researchers at frontier labs, he says, most employers now see engineers as oversupplied, and some worry that AI makes the surplus worse.
So employers spend less on pay, perks, and staff voice. John says this is a general pattern, not unique to Meta, and it makes being an employee rougher overall.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: Could weaker employee leverage also shape reorganization decisions?
answer: John agrees. Earlier Meta did many things that were bad for the business but made sense for keeping talent, and the company is doing less of that now. He says the fear of layoffs is the biggest emotional stressor for most people, more than perks such as food. After layoffs, people who had complained about losing perks became more tolerant of losing them.

He says MSL feels more stressful than some other frontier labs because layoffs seem possible there. The captions make his comparison with OpenAI and Anthropic hard to follow, so it is not restated here.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Did the promise of career growth change as a retention tool at Meta?
answer: John says many Meta divisions stopped talking about pay, purpose, and enjoying the work as reasons to stay. People instead said the only reason to do anything was a clear story about a promotion. When he moved from data infrastructure into AI infrastructure, he found almost no one whose first goal was not promotion.

Monetization was the strongest case. It hired people out of AI infrastructure with detailed plans for getting promoted. John says that worked for promotions but wrecked many teams, including several he later managed and had to repair. People on those teams agreed the work was bad and unlikely to succeed, yet shipped it to meet their promotion bar.

He says this made good software decisions almost impossible, and that the skills that would help careers most became separate from promotions. When the market turned against employees, managers told people to fear layoffs more than they hoped for promotions. He does not think that was a good cultural fix, though he sees it as an attempt to undo earlier damage.

followups.question: Did you see people keep playing the promotion game even when they saw unusual behavior?
answer: John says unless a VP is ready to fix the culture and shut it down, people have to play along. He calls not playing the game irrational, because one person cannot unilaterally disarm. He says the culture was dominant in AI infrastructure and monetization, was bad for nearly everyone, and left people in a demoralizing rat race.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: What could someone do about a culture like this?
answer: John says people have a lot of agency in choosing their team's culture. Meta had many teams without the promotion-first culture, PyTorch among them, where people worked for the love of the craft. Inside the system you still have to follow its rules, but you are not forced to stay in that machine. Not everyone would meet the bar for those teams, but many could.

He chose stable teams that would improve over time and keep a healthy culture, even though that meant slower promotion. He says he is torn. If the goal were lifetime earnings, fast-promoting and fast-firing teams might be economically rational. For him, enjoying the craft mattered more, and he was willing to accept about 20 percent less compensation to work somewhere he was prouder of.
followups.speaker: John White

followups.question: Did outsiders see PyTorch engineers as under-leveled?
answer: John says outsiders often believed PyTorch held a higher bar for promotion, which made it easier to convince others that PyTorch engineers were ready for higher levels. In hiring conversations, candidates sometimes asked whether PyTorch was under-leveled. John would say they might be, or that PyTorch held the right levels and the candidate had to decide whether to take a chance on them. He says PyTorch also trained people who became remarkably good.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: How was your early time at Facebook on the experimentation tools, before the promotion pressure?
answer: John says his first two years at Meta were some of his happiest, though also among the most frightening. He had asked for six months of leave to work on Julia, a language he was a core contributor to. While he was away, the manager who hired him left, and the team he had joined split into core data science and data science infrastructure.

He wanted to join core data science but worked closely with data science infrastructure, which owned the experimentation tools. He says that work was the most valuable thing he did as an individual contributor, and that people who know him from Meta remember him for it. Core data science was turbulent, with reorganizations, new managers, and churn.

A few months in, a paper from a research-leaning group that John was affiliated with became a major PR problem for Meta. John remembers it as something like 'Emotional Contagion in Social Networks'. He tried to prevent the problem but lacked the authority. The author later apologized to the company in a Q&A. John found himself in meetings with the head of legal, and his team faced the possibility of being disbanded. He calls it a formative experience, though the fallout faded.

Over the following years he became one of the main developers of Deltoid, its third iteration. When most senior engineers left within about six months, he became the only person who remembered how the system worked. At about IC5, he became a de facto tech lead and drove the vision for the A/B testing tools for years. He calls it some of the most fulfilling work he did at Meta.

followups.question: What was Deltoid, in short?
answer: John confirms that Deltoid is an A/B testing framework, where users are assigned to one code path or another and the team measures downstream effects. He says the Statsig product he knows looks almost identical to Deltoid in interface and features. He says he should have built a Deltoid-style startup years earlier, but lacked the wisdom to. He is not sure of Statsig's current state.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: What is Julia, and what was the data science language war about?
answer: John says he may have made Julia part of that war more than it needed to be. He argues that programming languages are products in zero-sum competition, and that saying otherwise misleads people. Julia's pitch was high-level code that reads like Python or MATLAB and still runs fast. MIT mathematicians designed it to replace MATLAB, so it targeted that market more than data science, though John helped push it toward data science.

His example is a distance-matrix function. The underlying C code is a set of plain loops, and a naive translation into R keeps the same loops, yet R runs far slower. John estimates 1,000 to 10,000 times slower than C. He was frustrated that many Python and R users treated speed as both impossible and unimportant. Julia rejected that view. John was a heavy R user and was disappointed by how often R fought him.

John says Julia has become less fashionable but is still doing well, and he believes it is among the top 25 languages by users. He thinks it is probably the only community still fighting that fight, even though he does not think it has won.

followups.question: What is the intuition behind R being about 10,000 times slower when the code looks similar to C?
answer: John says slow code usually does work it does not need to do. R pays a heavy overhead because it allows dynamic behavior that may never be used. In R, the brace used to mark a block can be redefined, so you must check whether it has changed. John says he may be misremembering whether it is braces or parentheses. Each such check can cost hundreds to thousands of machine cycles, while adding two 64-bit integers takes one.

R is also lazily evaluated, so function arguments become promise objects. John recalls a paper by two students and a senior professor, Jan Vitek, on the design of R. It found that most promises could have been evaluated eagerly, perhaps 70 to 90 percent, though he is not sure of the figure. Python's inspect module can also change the symbol table, so names cannot be trusted without checking. Fast languages have many guarantees, and R has very few.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Why did John find it frustrating that grad students and postdocs see industry as a safe fallback?
answer: John says what frustrated him most was that many PhD students wanted to be professors or postdocs, and treated industry as the fallback if they failed out. In interviews, some candidates clearly did not want to be there and saw the interview as a failure, which is not a good sign for an employer.

He also says many academics assumed industry jobs would be easy, as if smart people stayed in academia and weaker people went to industry. One candidate, effectively a computer science professor, could not pass values between functions in code. They printed values in a REPL, read them, and retyped them by hand. John says that method would not work for production code, and that the belief hurts students across the academic system.
blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Why does John hold such strong views on statistics, and which books does he recommend?
answer: John says he loves statistics but calls it one of the craziest fields. It sells the idea that statistical methods work in real life, yet much of the work is pure mathematics about idealized settings. In pure math, a proof only has to be internally consistent. In applied fields such as software, it is enough that the code runs. He says statistics reasons mathematically and then makes practical claims, and that is where opinions come in.

He says some statisticians hold themselves to a very high bar, while others call a claim true because they said so. His top recommendation is Larry Wasserman, whose books he calls the embodiment of intense honesty. Wasserman states what is assumed and what is implied, and avoids claims that are not true. John says no book has been better for learning statistics. He also recommends a book he recalls as something like Introduction to Agnostic Statistics, by an author the captions render as 'Peter Eranell'. He calls that author hyper-rigorous, and says the book is a little less math-heavy than Wasserman's, which suits social scientists and practitioners.

followups.question: Do people in industry approve launches on a green bar without checking the statistics underneath?
answer: John agrees and gives an example from the Deltoid 3 launch. Deltoid 1 was still the default. A reviewer blocked the launch because a holdout that had been a statistically significant win was no longer significant under Deltoid 3, and the reviewer read that as a regression. John replied that it might be a regression, or it might be the truth, and that nobody knew which. The reviewer wanted to wait until the half ended and goals were met. John argued that a result that close to the line is not a real win, since mild code changes could flip it.

John calls it a dangerous culture to treat results that barely cross or miss the significance line as clear wins or failures. He describes a team he managed that shipped code to hit a goal, although it planned to delete the code a day into the next half. He asked why they were shipping it, and they said they could not miss their goals. He argued that goals should not reward shipping code that will be deleted right away. He convinced them not to ship, since as the manager he decided ratings.
John says weak statistical understanding feeds other odd evaluation habits, and the two together become especially dangerous.
followups.speaker: John White

blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: Do you have a regret that others could learn from?
answer: John says he has a stock answer, because he is asked often. For his first several years, his skip-level manager, Javi, ran office hours. John's manager, Danny, kept suggesting that someone should go. John did not go, because he felt he had nothing valuable to say to Javi.

Later, as John ran office hours for a larger organization, he wished people would come, and he realized Javi had felt the same way. John says he missed a valuable opportunity and made things worse for Javi as well. He calls it a decision made out of fear that harmed both parties.

His advice for junior engineers is to go when a leader says they want to hear from people. Directors and above are far removed from the work, and John says he sometimes had managers managing managers. Bring a concrete idea rather than asking how to get promoted, he says. Leaders welcome that, and many people are afraid to do it, which makes everyone worse off.
blocks.speaker: John White

blocks.question: If you could go back to the start of your career and give yourself advice, what would you say?
answer: John says he holds strong opinions but can be more self-conscious than he should. His advice is to believe that bigger work is possible, and that with high discipline it is. From high school through college, he says, he too often cast doubt on what he could do. He calls that the biggest set of mistakes he has made: not being ambitious enough, or not believing a problem was tractable.

He also says people over-convince themselves of others' greatness and under-convince themselves of what they can achieve. That combination makes them take fewer risks than they could. Until he worked with many people who succeeded, he says, he did not see how often those people were not much better. They just tried, and others did not. For a 20-year-old version of himself, that is the main lesson he would give.
blocks.speaker: John White
